lesson.child_mission: Creating a digital presentation means few words per slide, strong headings and images that support—not decorate—the research message.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same strategy to an unfamiliar topic or audience, then compare the effect of two different choices.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Which slide is stronger for findings: a paragraph wall or three short bullets?

FEEDBACK
Three short bullets listeners can track while you speak.

CHECK
Animations that distract from facts weaken the presentation.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Build a 3–4 slide deck for your project. Label each slide’s job and one honesty check (no decorative contradicting images).

Write a short reflection describing one specific revision you made and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Creating a digital presentation means few words per slide, strong headings and images that support—not decorate—the research message.
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.

Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Build a 3–4 slide deck for your project. Label each slide’s job and one honesty check (no decorative contradicting images). Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Likely misconception: Animations that distract from facts weaken the presentation. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating digital on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with digital, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

teach_steps.explain:
Creating a digital presentation means few words per slide, strong headings and images that support—not decorate—the research message.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make decisions based on specific language evidence, rather than guess or copy someone else. Keep the meaning accurate and explain the choice.

HOW TO WORK
Read the original example and locate the words or actions that support the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Check your response against the feedback: did you address the same skill and show your reasoning? If a detail is uncertain, identify what would have to be checked. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than making the answer longer.
